card.headline: Another word for and
card.sub: also · too · plus · as well as · in addition · moreover

beats.role: answer on screen at 0:00 (H104) + open loop (closed in the moreover tip)
beats.speech: Another word for and? Also, too, plus, as well as, in addition, and moreover. Ten words: five for speaking and five for writing. And stay for a comma mistake that many learners make with moreover.

beats.label: everyday English
beats.chapter: Another word for and in speaking
beats.speech: Part one. Five words for everyday English.

card.headline: Also
card.meaning: and, in addition (neutral, usually before the main verb)
card.example: She speaks French. She also speaks Spanish.

beats.speech: Also. It adds one more thing, and it usually goes before the main verb. She speaks French. She also speaks Spanish.

card.headline: Too
card.meaning: also (everyday, at the end of the sentence)
card.example: I love pizza. My brother loves it too.

beats.speech: Too. It means also, and it goes at the end of the sentence. I love pizza. My brother loves it too.

card.headline: Plus
card.meaning: and also (casual, adds one more reason)
card.example: The flat is cheap, plus it's near the station.

beats.speech: Plus. It adds one more reason. It's casual, so use it when you speak. The flat is cheap, plus it's near the station.

card.headline: As well as
card.meaning: and also (neutral, often before a noun)
card.example: We sell coffee as well as tea.

beats.speech: As well as. It means and also, and it fits both speaking and writing. We sell coffee as well as tea.

card.headline: Along with
card.example: He sent flowers, along with a card.

beats.speech: Along with. It means together with. He sent flowers, along with a card.

card.headline: Also or too?
card.sub: She also speaks Spanish.  ·  She speaks Spanish too.

beats.speech: Also or too? Same meaning, different place. Also goes before the verb: she also speaks Spanish. Too goes at the end: she speaks Spanish too.

card.headline: Which one fits?
card.question: I like tea. My sister likes it ___.
card.answer: I like tea. My sister likes it too.
card.note: also = before the verb: she also likes it

beats.speech: I like tea. My sister likes it blank. Too, or also? | Too. At the end of the sentence, we say too.

card.headline: Which one fits?
card.question: The room is tiny, ___ it's very expensive.
card.answer: The room is tiny, plus it's very expensive.

beats.speech: The room is tiny, blank it's very expensive. Plus, or moreover? | Plus. It's casual, and it can join two parts of one sentence.

card.headline: Say it now
card.sentences:
She also speaks Spanish.
My brother loves it too.
It's cheap, plus it's near the station.

beats.speech: Now say it with me. Listen, then repeat. | She also speaks Spanish. | My brother loves it too. | It's cheap, plus it's near the station.

beats.label: formal writing
beats.chapter: Another word for and in writing
beats.speech: Part two. Five words for essays, emails and reports.

card.headline: In addition
card.meaning: also, one more fact (formal and neutral)
card.example: In addition, the hotel has a free gym.

beats.speech: In addition. It adds one more fact, and it works in any formal text. In addition, the hotel has a free gym.

card.headline: Additionally
card.example: Additionally, all rooms have free Wi-Fi.

beats.speech: Additionally. It means in addition. It's formal, so it's good for emails and reports. Additionally, all rooms have free Wi-Fi.

card.headline: Furthermore
card.meaning: and also, adds a further point (formal)
card.example: The plan is cheap. Furthermore, it is fast.

beats.speech: Furthermore. It adds a further point to an argument. It's formal. The plan is cheap. Furthermore, it is fast.

card.headline: Moreover
card.meaning: and also, adds a stronger point (very formal)
card.example: The method is simple. Moreover, it saves time.

beats.speech: Moreover. It adds a point that is even stronger. It's very formal, so keep it for writing. The method is simple. Moreover, it saves time.

card.headline: Besides
card.meaning: and anyway, adds one last reason (less formal)
card.example: I'm too tired to go out. Besides, it's raining.

beats.speech: Besides. It adds one last reason, often to say no. It's less formal than the others, so use it in emails, not essays. I'm too tired to go out. Besides, it's raining.

And here's the comma mistake from the start. Don't join two sentences with moreover and a comma. Write a full stop, then moreover, then a comma. It's cheap. Moreover, it's fast. The same goes for furthermore and in addition.

card.headline: Plus in an essay?
card.sub: In speech: plus  ·  In an essay: in addition

beats.speech: Can you use plus in an essay? Better not. Plus is casual. In an essay, write in addition or furthermore instead.

card.headline: Which one fits?
card.question: The report is clear. ___, it is well researched.
card.answer: The report is clear. Moreover, it is well researched.

beats.speech: The report is clear. Blank, it is well researched. Moreover, or plus? | Moreover. This is formal writing, and plus is too casual here.

card.headline: Which one fits?
card.question: I don't want to go. ___, it's too late.
card.answer: I don't want to go. Besides, it's too late.

beats.speech: I don't want to go. Blank, it's too late. Besides, or along with? | Besides. It adds one last reason. Along with needs a noun after it.

card.headline: Don't use one in every sentence
card.sub: Use them now and then, not in every line.

beats.speech: One more tip. Don't start every sentence with moreover or furthermore. It makes you sound like a robot. Often, a simple and is the best word.
